Our findings indicate that atomic gas dominates the nebula surrounding the jet, outweighing regions dominated by thermal ionization. Despite this, we note a lack of correlation between jet movement velocities and the column density of atomic material. Overall, these data underscore the critical role played by magnetic fields in governing jet dynamics and subsequent evolution.

This article employs a time-virtual regression framework incorporating time-exponential Factor Loadings functions derived from daily death counts across multiple age cohorts in the United States. Neural architecture search (NAS) aims to automatically discover efficient architectures for various machine learning tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce an interference-reduction method based on a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classifier. This approach predicts architecture performance using limited data to enable early filtering of low-potential designs before extensive training time is wasted. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our strategy, showing a performance improvement of up to 10% over existing baselines.

This study employs both time-resolved and time-averaged numerical approaches to analyze the mechanism behind laser-induced pattern formation when the laser beam enters a liquid medium. By calculating the time-evolution of the laser-induced temperature field based on the absorbed laser power density and the liquid's thermal, optical, and physical properties, we derived both the time-varying and long-term averaged distributions. Using this simulated temperature profile, we computed the corresponding refractive index variations, which successfully generated the characteristic self-diffraction patterns. To elucidate the underlying physics visualized in these patterns, we examined the relationship between the two methods of simulating and visualizing the data alongside our results on how the laser's wavelength and energy influence the time-resolved and steady-state temperature profiles. We established that the two fundamental self-diffraction mechanisms are driven by different physical processes: ring-like ring structures stem from transient thermal expansion, whereas six-armed diffraction spots arise from steady-state, self-induced convection currents.

Design dialogues involving human-computer interaction, often facilitated by software capable of interpreting user instructions to execute design tasks, have become increasingly prevalent. By enabling designers to access robust textual insights directly from their own projects, this method facilitates a accessible mining of what specific outcomes result from specific design parameters.

We present Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR), a framework designed to render photorealistic and interactive first-person views featuring moving virtual avatars interacting with their surroundings, targeting applications in AR, VR, and mixed reality. By utilizing an image-based technique that models data within a neural radiance field framework, our method captures appearance alongside motion, geometry, and lighting for multiple skeletons in various environments. To support wide user customization and distinct individual characteristics, the system decomposes motion into motion priors derived from exemplar videos and learnable pose adaptivities determined by a representative encoder; this separates long-term and short-term movement characteristics into distinct networks capable of handling both dynamic object interactions and simple pose alterations like walking or looking. We evaluated our techniques through extensive user studies and demonstrate superior quality compared to state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics.

The widespread adoption of image enhancement tools has drastically changed the digital image ecosystem, yet little is known regarding how these alterations impact digital recognition systems. This study bridges that gap by demonstrating that humans and digital image analysis algorithms—specifically those related to face verification—react differently to intense image modification. While humans often focus on face shapes, even under stress, machines struggle significantly as alterations trigger false rejections regarding face matching. Consequently, although these technologies differ in sensitivity to visual changes, this divergence underscores a critical area for further investigation into their robustness.

The paper investigates the connection between Chern-Simons theory and the Askey-Wilson algebra. It begins by examining how topological quantum field theories are tied to integrable systems, a relationship that emerges from an analysis of the isomorphism between the braid group and the centralizer of a regular semisimple element within a Weyl group. Utilizing this framework, we constructs topological quantum field theories rooted in the Askey-Wilson algebra. We further analyze quantum field theories derived from the Chern-Simons action and formulate link invariants in terms of the spin representation of the Askey-Wilson algebra. This study employs cluster quantum Monte Carlo techniques to analyze the ground states of 2D frustrated magnetic systems characterized by trimers with antiferromagnetic bonds embedded in a host lattice with weak couplings. Specifically, these findings are applied to the $A$-site framework of the kagome ferromagnets $YbFePO_5$ and $YbFePO_7$. In the strong-coupling regime, the ground state is known to be the cluster ferromagnetic state, where each trimer functions as a single $S=1/2$ spin aligned with the planes, which interacts via effective exchange mechanisms. Furthermore, this study examines the phase's stability against the alternative vacuum configuration, where each trimer remains in a cluster valence bond state.

The success of language models in natural-linguistic tasks, such as natural-language inference (NIL), heavily depends on specific prompts, which often necessitate model fine-tuning. This limitation is particularly evident in the zero-shot setting for NL I, where prompt engineering typically requires fine-tuning, a step that restricts model flexibility and limits the number of usable prompts. An effective solution lies in expanding the pool of trainable parameters for prompt-adjacent inputs without compromising prompt quality or the train-ability of the prompt system. This method achieves expansion by incorporating extra parameters dedicated to modulating the output distributions at a per-classification-task scope. This technique enhances the trainable range of hint-prompt combinations in a model's vocabulary to achieve zero-shot success. By applying meta-learning principles to this expanded architecture, we can further refine these classification-task hooks to achieve a more efficient fine-tuning process. This expanded meta-structure allows the system to learn a broader spectrum of hint-partial pairings, which enables the model to generalize better across and perform more effectively on zero NL IP tasks.

We propose an oscillation model to explain the recurrent, variable emission from low-mass active galactic nuclei (specifically those with $0.01-0.1\,M_{\odot}$ black holes). In this scenario, emission is generated by accreting material striking the inner regions of a system consisting of a black hole and a compact, dense orbiting body. This configuration is hypothesized to represent the early phase of body formation, including processes like protoplanetary disk formation, ring formation within tidal disruption events, systems involving compact objects, or bodies that have been directly swallowed by the black hole. In such systems, the orbital timescale of the secondary object dictates the oscillation period. When the orbital period closely matches the timescale for thermal instability in the inner accretion flow, oscillations can be amplified into pronounced outbursts. Consequently, the resulting light curves mimic those of outbursts in supermassive black hole binaries. These proposed mechanisms could account for observed phenomena, including the observed outburst from the low-mass active galactic nucleus 2M1237, as well as oscillation features detected in the nuclear regions of the galaxy NGC 1068 and the binary NGC 7469.

This finding supports the hypothesis of a multipolar field configuration, which may explain the observed asymmetry in the magnetic moment seen in the star's light distribution.

This study introduces a non-invasive method for estimating epidemic-related dynamics without relying on invasive data collection. Observer design serves as the core mechanism to approximate essential variables, utilizing only accessible, non-invasive measurements. U-shaped, E-shaped, and E-shaped observers are developed and validated using the SEIR epidemic model. Predicting future entity relationships is a critical task across numerous data-driven applications, ranging from visual question answering and interactive knowledge graph user simulation to interactive chatbots and software agents. This paper presents an efficient, high-performance method for predicting these relationships by integrating three static neural architectures to produce the final prediction. Specifically, this approach aggregates structural insights from a knowledge graph's historical topology, rich contextual information from its entity descriptions, and temporal patterns derived from relationship evolution. Empirical evaluations on three standard benchmarks demonstrate that modeling relationships through multi-source static embeddings significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art dynamic, temporal linkage methods. Our findings confirm that incorporating descriptive entity context is a key driver for success, offering a superior alternative to relying solely on temporal dynamics. Consequently, methods combining static embeddings with temporal cues achieve state-of-the-art results in link forecasting. This study also highlights the value of efficient task-specific modeling, which enables the development of systems with the potential to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices.

Optical oscillators utilizing mode-locking at the femtosecond timescale have become indispensable for generating peak powers in ultrafast laser applications, especially for applications involving nonlinear spectroscopy and plasma creation. The foundational mechanism governing mode-locking in passively stable oscillators is the Kerr-lens effect; however, despite the field's maturity and long-standing use of this technique, a rigorous quantitative link between the geometric properties of the phase and amplitude transmission masks and the resulting pulse characteristics remains absent. To address this, the text introduces an analytical framework for non-dimensionalizing phase parameters in the context of passive mode-locking dynamics. This approach facilitates a systematic investigation into how the shapes amplitude and phase influence pulse observables, revealing insights into the interplay between these masks and laser performance metrics. Furthermore, the study applies this new framework to characterize an operational oscillatory system, offering guidance for optimizing the design of future high-peak-power femtosecond optical sources.

This study investigates regression challenges where data is scattered across numerous resource-limited IoT devices capable of executing deep neural networks for feature extraction prior to a global model performing the final nonlinearity. We establish an asynchronous global update scheme that accommodates the varying computational speeds and data distributions of clients while mitigating the bias induced by limited local data. We evaluate both theoretically and empirically that our method surpasses existing approaches requiring test-time interactions with the server, making it well-suited for extensive IoT deployments.

Recent advancements in silicon-based microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) have enabled the fabrication of high-quality silicon membranes as thin as a few hundred nanometers, promising a path toward integrating optical and electronic functions in future silicon photonics applications. However, such thin membranes suffer from inadequate light absorption, prompting this study to explore the use of three-dimensional (3D) photonic band gap (PBG) structures as rear reflectors. These structures trap photons within the membrane, enhancing overall absorption across both visible and infrared ranges. This SR format consolidates diverse annotations—including diagnostic reports, pixel-level segmentation data, and model outputs—into a single, transferable SR file. *Highdicom* further enables bidirectional conversion between the multi-layer DICOM SR format and Python's pandas data structures, facilitating seamless data processing. The Python code for generating data annotations and frameworks is available at https://highdicom.readthedocs.io/ and can be accessed via https://highdicom.readthedocs.io/.

Deep learning techniques have recently gained prominence in genomic research for their capacity to uncover intricate sequence motifs in DNA. However, existing approaches are typically dependent on substantial annotated data, requiring the classification of specific genomic regions (such as promoters or enhancers) prior to the extraction of relevant motifs. We introduce a method for discovering sequence motifs within a single unlabeled dataset that demands no prior human insight or parameter configuration. Our technique utilizes a pretrained language model specifically trained to assign probabilities to nucleotide sequences. This model is refined by enhancing its scoring capability through the HRON (DNN-based) architecture, which incorporates various types of contextual features. These features are constructed by processing the genomic sequences using multiple mononucleotide alphabets. We demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms the baseline model on the DNA1000 benchmark. Notably, our method's efficacy stems from its ability to generate sequences that closely resemble those found in the training data rather than from detecting specific biological functions.

Thin film versions of Mott insulators offer readily accessible model systems for investigating metal-insulator transitions (MITs). Through a comprehensive analysis of $V_2O_3$(001) films with atomic-scale thickness grown on $GdO_x/Bi_2O_2Se$ substrates, this work examines the correlation between the MIT and metallic characteristics of the surface layer. A $T_{\rm{MIT}}$ reduction is observed as film thickness decreases, yet this shift is not fully accounted for by quantum confinement. Instead, the study finds that a volatile $T_{\rm{MET}}$ in the surface monolayer competes with the bulk transition, ultimately driving the shift in $T_{\rm{MIT}}$.

We present the findings of a systematic search for planetary orbit irregularities among KMT-Net planets observed during the 2018 eclipse using a uniform, efficient algorithm. This absence of dynamical activity among nominally stable planets contrasts with observations of similar systems by other researchers and may stem from specific limitations inherent to our search methodology.

To address how to leverage spatial orientation for image recognition, this paper introduces Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCN). Unlike isotropic image classification, the OCN architecture applies orientation-based filtering and orientation-based convolution, thereby learning robust representations that incorporate directional information. Specifically, OCNs consist of an orientation-based filtering layer that decomposes an input image into oriented filters capturing directional patterns, followed. by orientation-based convolutional layers designed to aggregate spatial information respecting orientation invariance. Comprehensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy over both standard convolutional networks (CNNs) and their orientation-based counterparts (OB-Net), highlighting OCNs ability model intricate spatial relationships within images. Detailed evaluations on image classification tasks further highlight OCNs capacity for extracting potent spatial features across diverse datasets.

In 2019, a new coronavirus emerged, causing over 75 million infections and 4 million deaths globally. While vaccines and treatments are still under development, lung CT imaging is currently used to detect the virus. However, existing radiologists are overwhelmed, and the lack of consistent imaging protocols and varying image qualities have made automated machine learning models difficult to develop. This study introduces a novel, two-stage deep learning system for detecting the virus from low-dose CT scans. The system utilizes an optimized Two-pair Pairwise Pairwise loss function and a specialized deep learning model called Time-distributed Capsule Networks (TDNC). Evaluation on a dataset of 1,040 low-dose CT scans achieved a sensitivity of 99% and a specificity of 95%. The results demonstrate that the proposed system can perform at a level comparable to experienced human radiologists.

This study assesses the current availability of low-Earth orbit (LEO) space, concentrating on highly valuable regions within the LEO spectrum. We modeled LEO availability as a continuous function across altitude and inclination, integrating orbital dynamics, in-situ debris flux, and concurrent satellite populations within those parameters. Our analysis indicates that LEO remains largely unconstrained above 400 km for most latitudes greater than approximately 30 degrees, whereas available space is markedly lower at inclinations less than 30 degrees. Consequently, we anticipate heightened commercial activity within the zone spanning 550 km to 800 km at inclitudes between 30 degrees and 40 degrees. This surge in LEO utilization within this specific corridor may precipitate a substantial rise in satellite debris, posing heightened risks to other active satellites. Ultimately, we explore how the widespread adoption of high-altitude LEOs could drive the acceleration of satellite-storm mitigation and collision-avoidance methodologies.

This optimization framework ensures a robust and reliable grid generation process.

Recommendation systems (RS) are essential for assisting users in discovering products and services online. However, their recommendations are often opaque and can sometimes appear unreasonable, prompting interest in explanations that clarify the "why" behind these suggestions. Specifically, Local Interpretable Model-Embedded Explanation (LIME) has emerged as an attractive local explanation method for RS due to its versatility across systems with varying feature sets. LIME generates explanations by modeling a target RS as a sparse, weight-based linear function. While standard LIME is flexible regarding the input data distribution, it lacks constraints on the relationship between sample datasets used for explanation and the item's actual distribution. This absence of a commitment to a specific distribution can result in unstable explanations that vary depending on the random samples selected. This paper introduces the Commitment-LIME framework, which forces models to demonstrate stability by making them commit to a specific distribution for sample usage. Commitment-LIME incorporates an additional regularization term designed to guarantee this commitment; we prove mathematically that this ensures exactly one valid solution exists for any given explanation request. Experimental evaluations confirm that our approach yields significantly more stable explanations compared to the baseline LIME model.

This paper presents a thorough investigation of Fermi level pinning in InAs quantum wells situated near the surface of a GaAs substrate. By examining devices with various GaAs cap layer thicknesses, we demonstrate that the Fermi level position is not solely dictated by metal-semiconductor work function alignment but is significantly controlled by the number of InAs monolayers exposed to GaAs. Specifically, increasing the InAs quantum well thickness shifts the Fermi level upward, whereas cap layer variations have a more pronounced effect when the InAs layer is thin. This behavior is explained by an enhanced sensitivity of thin InAs wells to hole-to-surface state transfer, causing the electronic band structure to stabilize closer to that of the GaAs matrix rather than retaining the InAs character. This mechanism is corroborated by high-resolution photoluminescence and temperature-dependent capacitance-voltage (C-V) measurements. Furthermore, the C-V data indicate that thin InAs quantum wells are heavily p-type. This finding suggests that near-surface InAs quantum wells can be effectively utilized as p-doping layers in GaAs heterostructure devices.

The interaction between a superconducting reservoir and a quantum dot serves as a foundational setup for superconducting hybrid devices, yet the nature of the tunneling dynamics driving this coupling remains elusive. We present an active gate-tunneling technique that allows us to track, in real-time, the movement of electrons and holes between the two entities—a capability that passive gate monitoring lacks due to its inability to capture such tunneling events effectively. Our analysis reveals that, unlike electrons, the tunneling of holes exhibits pronounced dependence on the gate voltage, whereas electron transport remains largely constant. Furthermore, the dynamics associated with gate manipulation demonstrate that both particles and holes can simultaneously occupy the quantum dot relative to a superconducting ground state, consistent with the predicted effects of Andreev reflection. The observed hysteresis in active gate control is attributed to the interaction between the tunneling rates and the energy levels within the quantum-relaxation regime. Ultimately, this research advances gate-tunneling methods and offers a viable pathway for using real-time gate sensing to investigate the behavior of superconducting ground states in hybrid superconductor-semiconductor systems.

Conservative vector fields play a central role in formulating physical laws across diverse domains of mathematics and science. We examine a specific class of frameworks for conservation laws governed by these fields, utilizing entropic discontinuents defined by jump curves with vertical tangents. By applying concepts from relative entropy to generate constraints on these discontinuents, we derive entropic conditions that these solutions must meet. We prove that the conditions derived are both necessary and sufficient for a function to represent solutions to the corresponding conservation laws, thereby establishing their characterizations as the unique solutions satisfying these entropic criteria within a specific function class. We further investigate how to compute contraction maps that transform one entropic solution to another, demonstrating they exist under certain requirements and providing practical methods to determine them using maps derived from a variational principle.

This study presents a technique for generating hypertext-to-speech (TTS) synthesis based on median values, which is particularly suitable for text-dependent tasks. We also describe an experimental validation of the procedure, comparing the results with traditional statistical approaches. The findings indicate that the median-value method and the associated training process are more effective for text-dependent speech synthesis, resulting in higher-quality final outputs.

Comprising 100 million samples of 1.5 Teb by size, these repositories hold significantly greater volume and complexity than most existing training sets. This study introduces a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture designed to handle both global context and local details within deep learning models. Directed topology offers a robust framework for addressing the fundamental issue of temporal directionality, a deficiency found in classical topological theories. We demonstrate that all super- and semilinear versions constitute valid directed topological spaces. Furthermore, we investigate the continuity relationships linking these various spaces. Finally, we outline key aspects of a computer science application for this topological theory.

In recent years, deep learning has become a dominant force in medical image analysis, offering superior accuracy and efficiency. However, developing robust models for tasks like categorization and segmentation remains difficult due to issues such as data scarcity, high computational demands, and annotation noise. While limited data can often be mitigated by data augmentation, deep learning-based segmentation and categorization are significantly hampered by label noise, often resulting in models that fail to generalize effectively. This study introduces the Bayesian Statistics Directed Label Renovation Mechanism (BS- LRM), a technique designed to reduce label noise specifically for medical image categorization. By leveraging a binary Bayesian statistics framework, the method identifies samples with high uncertainty and applies targeted renovations to correct label noise within those samples. Experimental evaluations across two publicly available datasets confirm the method's effectiveness, demonstrating substantial improvements in categorical accuracy.

**Interpolation** plays a central role in numerous fields of mathematics and scientific inquiry. There are various forms of interpolation available, each differing based on the type of data being used—for instance, classical interpolation relies on function values, whereas spline collocation uses derivative information. A key focus within these methods is the interpolation operator, $L$, associated with a given set of nodes, $\mathbf{x}$. The norm of this operator depends on $\mathbf{x}$ and tends to become unbounded as this norm grows without limit. Historically, researchers have sought upper limits for this numerical value. Previous studies by various authors have addressed these bounds in standard interpolation contexts. In this work, we investigate particular cases of $L$. The outcome provides an explicit formula for this norm in specific scenarios. Our findings also provide counter-examples to a conjecture proposed by M. de la Cal and J. M. Ramos, which claimed a sharp upper bound valid for all possible sets. Furthermore, we introduce notation for relevant subsets of these solution spaces.

We examine a continuous-time random walk on the vertices of a weighted, undirected, and connected simple graph, linking a specific transition probability matrix to a monic, irreducible, distinctively defined characteristic polynomial. We also explore the connections between this matrix and the corresponding Markov chain, providing complementary findings and positioning these results to facilitate future applications in spectral graph theory.

Estimating the genus of graphs is NP-hard, as established by both its significance in algorithmic complexity and its applications in topological data analysis. This difficulty stems primarily from the $O(n^3)$ time complexity required by the most efficient existing approximation approach by Duffus et al., which is often prohibitive for large datasets. In this work, we demonstrate how to drastically reduce this computational burden when estimating the genus of graphs where edge density is either constant or linear. We introduce an effective method that achieves polynomial-time performance, specifically operating in $O(n^2 \log n)$ time, while delivering genus estimates with high accuracy across constant or linear graphs.

We introduce a randomized Newton method designed for distributed convex optimization in networks, targeting the network-wide minimization of jointly separable objectives. Our proposed approach operates by iteratively computing the search direction using the inverse of the aggregate Hessian and updating the solution via a consensus process that incorporates a step-size scaling factor. We prove convergence for a broad range of step parameters and demonstrate how efficiently it accelerates consensus attainment. Most distinctively, we establish an exact analytical upper bound on the total computational complexity. Our experimental results confirm that, for various step parameters, our method significantly surpasses standard centralized Newton algorithms in both real and simulated distributed settings.

In addition, this research provides a thorough analysis of the strengths and limitations of various models in order to establish a firm foundation for future work in the field.

Additionally, "recoil tail" signatures from protons and alpha particles are detected, while simultaneously measuring scattered particle recoil energy through ionization calibration. This system, designed for background-free recoil event study, aims to investigate rare-rare processes such as neutrino-proton scattering, sterile neutrino production, double electron capture, and the search for dark matter particles interacting via weak force.

In recent years, there has been a marked increase in machine learning research aimed at creating contextual smart choice algorithms capable of making decisions comparable to those of human experts. Despite these advancements, real-world datasets are scarce, hindering both the validation of methods and the achievement of practical success due to challenges in recruiting sufficient training experts and defining contextual factors. This paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes automatically extracted contexts—specifically, the driving behaviors of trailer drivers—to supervise comparisons between machine learning outputs and human decisions for a fair evaluation of commercial driving performance. Our smart contextual expert system determines whether a driver can successfully navigate through obstacles by analyzing the vehicle's path relative to barriers and the movements made by a specified truck. Data derived from 110 driving videos involving 10 professional drivers have been employed to identify key contextual factors and develop algorithms that compare automated results with human judgments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms a standard tracker by more than 10\% in AUC scores when accounting for the difficulty ratings assigned by expert drivers.

This video demonstrates the Periodized Length Count Suture Anchor Fixation System. Traditional anchor techniques rely on the surgeon pulling suture material through sequentially placed holes within the anchor, pulling out sutures like "cheese strings." In this traditional method, every additional anchor requires an extra step, as the last suture must be manually extracted. In contrast, the current method allows all three horizontal sutures to pass through a single hole within the anchor without pulling them individually. Sutures are tensioned using length-counting instruments, wherein sutures become progressively longer as tension is incrementally increased. Once fully tensioned, sutures pass over the bone and into the tendon, where pass-by-pass length measurements indicate consistent increments of force. Sutures remain tensioned by locking them with a button placed over the instrument. Once tension is set, sutures are cut and excess ends trimmed before tying them together. Ultimately, this technique provides more reproducible fixation compared to traditional methods, which can vary depending on surgeon skill factors such as pulling force or knot patterns introduced when tightening sutures manually. Additionally, this approach reduces the risk of complications, including tear or fracture of the tendon caused by sutures that are pulled too forcefully during manual extraction.

This article introduces an approximate theoretical framework designed to investigate the ionization of one- and two-electron systems within a strong DC environment. Building upon the concept of outward complex scaling, which has historically facilitated theoretical atomic and molecular ionization studies, this method allows the stationary Schrödinger equation to extend into high-energy continuum segments. Crucially, unlike standard complex scaling that rotates all coordinates, this approach rotates them independently. Consequently, the resulting complex-rotated eigenfunctions represent discrete bound states adjacent to specific high-energy continuum segments. Validations demonstrate that the calculated phase shifts for hydrogen align closely with experimental measurements or unrotated scattering results, while energy stability analysis yields accurate resonance parameters for these states. Furthermore, targeting a high-energy resonance in a one-electron helium-like ion and a low-energy resonance in helium by rotating coordinates, this method offers new perspectives on the problem. Additionally, it is demonstrated that outward bi-fork rotation of complex angles in a hydrogen-like atom consistently converges to real total energies for all scaling parameters, regardless of scale size. This finding suggests that outward bi-fork rotation may also converge to real total energies for multi-electron atoms and potentially other systems.

This study presents a measurement of the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy ($\sqrt{s}$) of 5.02 TeV, utilizing data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC during 2015. The analysis isolates events in the dilepton channel, specifically targeting final states containing two muons or one electron paired with one muon, relying on a data set that corresponds to an integrated luminosity of $6.8 \, \text{fb}^{-1}$. The top quark pair production cross-section is determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 6.75 \, \pm$ (AT) $0.22$ (stat) $\pm$ (syst) $0.22$ (SM) pb. Furthermore, the $k$-factor, representing the ratio between the calculated theoretical $k$-factor and the observed experimental $k$-factor, aligns well with Standard Model expectations.

The GUIDES (Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Data Solutions) initiative is an initiative of the European Union's Horizon 2020 program, serving as a collaborative project involving seven partners across four countries. Its primary objective is to facilitate the acquisition, acquisition, management, and analysis of diverse geospatial urban data. This need stems from the incompatibility, or siloed nature, of various standards and data formats utilized by numerous European city municipalities, which hinders effective use across different urban frameworks such as IFC, CityGML, OGC City Models, and 3D-TIGER. The GUIDES framework operates by converting these disparate source formats into a unified core representation, which is subsequently mapped into both CityGML and IFC, while also supporting the use of other additional models.
To enhance practical application and facilitate adoption by European municipalities, the project has established the GUIDES Suite—a comprehensive software suite comprising four key components: a data converter tool, an integrator for data harvesting and merging, a search-capable portal for data discovery and retrieval, and a specialized analysis engine tailored for geospatial urban information.

We introduce a state-independent dephasing technique that monitors spin states in trapped calcium ions, measuring how trap radiofrequency (RF) modes are heated by an external environment. These trap modes, which confine the ions, determine the strength of Coulomb interactions between them. Our method tracks dephasing relative to ions occupying specific trap mode eigenstates, revealing a clear correlation: higher excitation probabilities lead to faster dephasing. By analyzing this link, we extract the probability distributions of the heating states for each mode, achieving a fidelity of approximately 90% against numerically simulated reference distributions. The approach enables precise measurement of the average energy increase in trap modes, reaching sensitivities below 0.1K over observation periods of roughly 10 milliseconds. As an experimental tool, this technique facilitates rapid diagnostics and mitigation of trap mode heating, addressing a primary obstacle in developing long-lived, high-fidelity quantum memories based on trapped ions.

Terahertz Surface Termination Spectroscopy (TERS) is a powerful technique for investigating the electronic characteristics of surfaces with high precision. This study introduces a method that fully accounts for the interplay between chemical and electromagnetic factors, which is crucial for accurately explaining TERS data. The reliability of this method is validated through detailed analyses of the interaction between acetylacetone and a gold substrate, as well as a simple test case involving the molecular polarization of methanol.

Reinforcement learning theories describe the frequent tendency of individuals to abandon a failing option and adopt a more successful one via the processing of reward prediction errors. Conversely, when outcomes are particularly reinforcing, individuals often engage in additional trials beyond what basic reinforcement learning models predict. This study, involving a novel midbrain imaging technique, demonstrates that the region is highly responsive to particularly rewarding outcomes and that both behaviors—tendency to switch away from low-reward options and to continue high-reward ones—align with measured neural activity in the midbrain. These findings indicate that midbrain processing of reward intensity is a critical factor in understanding human learning strategies. Crucially, the magnitude of this neural response predicts individual differences in these exploration tendencies, as people exhibiting stronger midbrain encoding are more likely to exhibit non-bilinear patterns in their behavior that deviate from standard reinforcement learning frameworks.

Time series are increasingly common in data collection, serving to capture the evolution of information across many fields, including genomics, finance, and computer science. They are frequently visualized using the 1-dimensional profile (1DP), a tree-shaped structure where the x-axis represents time and node heights reflect the series' values. Distance between 1D profiles is typically measured using the Fréchet distance, which quantifies the minimal maximum distance between a path connecting two shapes. Although the 1DP transformation is effective, it suffers from a critical limitation: even with constant-width time series, the tree's degree can become exponentially large relative to the input size. This expansion creates a vast search space that renders current state-of-the-ne-neighbor methods under realistic constraints exponentially slow. Consequently, finding the next closest neighbor in 1D profiles is intractable. In this work, we examine how data topology—specifically the number of close neighbors—is governed by geometric attributes such as path length, tree degree, and branch width. We also analyze how strict bounds on these properties impact estimation accuracy and algorithmic speed for estimating the number neighbors in 1D profiles.

Algorithms designed to optimize the cost-efficiency of quantum computers frequently rely on Simulated Annealing, which addresses combinatorial optimization challenges by equating the system's sampling distribution to a Boltzmann distribution. By leveraging quantum mechanics-inspired annealing, these methods seek solutions that minimize algorithmic costs associated with circuit compilation, qubit mapping, and other problems. A primary obstacle for such algorithms is the measurement noise inherent to short-term quantum operations, which distorts and biases the sampling distribution, thus hindering the system's ability to approach the optimal quantum critical temperature. This study introduces an error-correction protocol that applies Bayesian inference to clean measurement outputs, thereby reducing biases and enhancing the algorithmic performance. The efficacy of this approach is validated on real quantum hardware using the Mapping Ising model for a Media Network Media Planning problem.

This paper demonstrates a method to communicate robot intentions effectively, achieving previously unmet goals regarding intention conveyance. We specifically aim to make a robot's capabilities comprehensible to humans. While existing research focuses heavily on predicting a robot's immediate actions to convey intent, these approaches often fail to address broader understanding. We propose instead a novel technique based on "shared autonomy," designed to align a robot's movements with the current human state. Key features of this approach include its adaptability to diverse human configurations and the reliance on shared autonomy to instill human trust in the robot. Experimental evaluations confirm that this shared autonomy strategy surpasses current state-of-the-art methodologies.

While navigation in uncharted environments is a crucial aspect of real-world robotics, it remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty of building accurate maps and localizing robots within them. Occupancy grid maps are widely used in exploration and navigation tasks; however, their high dimensionality often leads to suboptimal performance in real-time scenarios. Topological map-based methods offer an alternative by abstracting the environment into a compact graph, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Yet, topological representations typically lack the detailed spatial context required for effective operation in vast or unfamiliar settings. To address this limitation, we introduce a hybrid approach that integrates both topological and metric information through a new Hierarchical Topological Map (HiTMap). This model represents the environment using agent-level and map-level nodes captured via path descriptions and spatial sentences. We trained an end-to-end neural decoder on simulated data to convert partial observation sequences into the HiTMap structure. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that our method achieves superior real-time capabilities and maintains higher positional accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

This work presents a mathematically grounded approach for reconstructing and processing X-ray polyenergetic computed tomography (pCT) data, incorporating experimental noise and enabling material decomposition. The primary innovation is a new non-convex variational framework formulated on a Riemannian manifold that enhances X-ray imaging, reconstruction, noise reduction into specific materials, and the estimation of X-ray beam energy spectra—all without the need for calibration. By introducing calibration-free parameters, this model allows for greater flexibility in selecting reconstruction algorithms suited to various noise characteristics and data types. The proposed solution offers an unified, end-to-end strategy for processing raw CT images for material analysis, diverges from traditional methods requiring multiple scans, and demonstrates significantly higher accuracy in noise reduction compared to existing techniques by jointly handling spectral variation and noise simultaneously.

It is demonstrated that as the size of the optical gap shrinks, the spill-over of electrons and band nonlocality effects cause a shift of in-gap surface plasmons toward the vacuum side of the gap. An empirical formula is provided to calculate the new plasmon position, incorporating the contributions of both spill-over and nonlocal mechanisms. Additionally, in the limit where a metal is separated by a vacuum gap from a highly damped semiconductor, the classical limit for an ideal surface plasmon is predicted to be shifted to approximately 0.8 eV, or roughly the bulk plasmon frequency of the semiconductor.

This study investigates the effectiveness of a feedback mechanism designed to highlight important words, which serves to enhance context utilization in model-guided naming instance extraction systems. The underlying framework, named TSNEI, integrates a bidirectional LSTM with a switch, a conditional sequence selection unit, and a termsignificance module. While prior research has proposed various metrics for assessing word significance, we evaluate four such metrics—Z-Score, Mutual Information, Minimal Entropy Score, and Perplexity—within the NLP domain. The models, trained on the SemEval-2014 task for Named Entity Instances extraction, demonstrate that the Mutual Information score yields the most performance gains, surpassing prior state-of-the-art results.

Digital Health Record Systems (DHR) serve as a pivotal, expanding database for managing patient information. Given that most patients utilize DHRs for extended periods, this accumulation provides substantial data capable of supporting personalized medicine through the identification of patient similarities. However, within DHR, patient records are heterogeneous, incorporating diverse attributes like demographics, clinical history, and medication details. Standard similarity algorithms often fail because these methods struggle to account for both the quantity and heterogeneity of such attributes. To overcome this, the graph-based Deep Learning framework known as DSGN (Diverse Similarity GeNeRal Neural network) is introduced. DSGN is designed to accurately compare digital health records regardless of their length or content variety. Unlike many existing deep learning techniques, this specific model requires minimal feature engineering and does not necessitate large, annotated datasets for training validation. Consequently, the DSGN framework offers a highly versatile and robust tool for analyzing digital health records.

This study investigates how solvent polarization influences the structure of an electric double layer (EDL) at a charged soft interface using a one-dimensional mean-field framework. While previous investigations have largely neglected solvent polarization despite its known influence on various physical phenomena, this research explicitly models it by introducing a solvent dipole and incorporating its polarization effects into the Ornstein-Zernike equation via a frequency-dependent dielectric constant. Results indicate that increasing the solvent's polarization strength intensifies charge screening at the interface, thereby diminishing overall surface charge density. This effect competes with electrostatic interactions to establish the EDL structure, leading to a thinner double layer when a higher frequency-dependent dielectric constant is applied due to solvent polarization. Additionally, solvent polarization shifts the point of zero charge (PZC) toward zero surface potential and results in isotherms that deviate from standard Donnan equilibrium predictions. Ultimately, these findings underscore the necessity of accounting for solvent polarization when analyzing the architecture of electric double layers at soft interfaces.

We introduce an approach for deducing software specifications from unstructured documents. While existing methods rely on labeled datasets—a resource-intensive training resource—resulting in limited applicability—our method bypasses labeled data training entirely. Instead, it integrates abstract interpretation, a static analysis formalism for precise specification, with Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate semantic specifications. We evaluate two strategies: (1) prompting the LLM to explicitly describe a function's pre- and postconditions before generating the actual specification, and both techniques significantly outperform baseline models in effectiveness. We further explore their strengths and weaknesses, highlighting methodological insights.

This study presents an enhanced network coding approach within a cooperative multi-user framework. By enabling users to encode retrieved data packets themselves, the method significantly reduces the transmit power required by relays. The specific challenge addressed involves optimizing relaying assignment, power allocation, and transmission strategies to efficiently network-code data across multiple relays. The result is a set of closed-form solutions for optimal user and relay selection. The remaining power is then evenly distributed among users to ensure equal contribution. Finally, the efficacy of this design is validated through numerical simulations, which demonstrate that the network coding strategy achieves superior performance compared to standard non-network-coded scenarios.

In the realm of satellite imagery, numerous research studies have developed deep networks designed to identify edges within images. However, these methods are not only highly dependent on specific parameters but also suffer from increased computational costs. This study introduces an innovative, non-deep neural network (DNN)-free framework for edge detection that offers superior computational efficiency without relying on complex deep learning architectures. By drawing on principles from fractal geometry and dimensionality, the proposed technique calculates dimension-based features to identify edges, resulting in significant reductions in processing time compared to traditional deep networks while maintaining a comparable level of accuracy.

X-ray absorption edge spectroscopy is a versatile and precise method for characterizing the local electronic environments of atoms within a material. However, employing high-fluence X-ray beams can induce non-linear effects that distort spectra, thereby hindering data analysis. This work introduces a rate framework to model the kinetics of electron state transitions driven by multi-photon and field-ionization mechanisms. This approach is grounded in multi-photon and dielectric tunneling rate equations, enabling the simulation and interpretation of non-linear XA spectra across a broad spectrum of scenarios.

Although deep learning has achieved significant success in classifying small and medium-sized objects within industrial and medical imaging, these models remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. These attacks induce prediction errors triggered by minute, engineered perturbations designed to exploit model weaknesses. To address this challenge, we introduce a new, cost-free adversarial training technique that enhances modulation categorization resistance. Named BLEND-GAN (Blending Generative Adversarial Networks), this method leverages the generative capabilities of GANs to create data that mimics the characteristics of original datasets. By integrating both real samples from the source data set with adversarial examples generated by BLEND-GAN during the training process, the resulting model demonstrates heightened resilience to such attacks. Our results indicate that this approach yields a robust 90% clean accuracy on two distinct benchmarks: MoCo-Net and MoCo-Net Large. Furthermore, the technique demonstrates a remarkable 60% reduction in attack success rates compared to standard supervised training baselines.

Segmentation of brain lesions is a critical task across radiology and medical imaging. This research presents and evaluates techniques for training deep learning models across clinics specifically for multi-sclerosis lesion segmentation. The multi-clinic dataset comprises approximately 1,100 CT 3D scans from eight different facilities, containing roughly 5,100 manually annotated lesions. Utilizing a UNETR architecture enhanced by an adapter layer for domain adaptation, we contrast three approaches: randomly sampling training data (Approach A), exclusively using an organization's labels to fine-tune a pre-trained base model (Approach B), and continuously refining the base model with weighted data from all sites (Approach C). Evaluation metrics include Dice similarity coefficient, sensitivity, and area under the curve. Results indicate that the baseline approach (A) performs poorly on test sets from non-participating sites, yielding low AUC scores between 0.59 and 0.69. In contrast, all adaptive strategies significantly boost cross-site performance, elevating AUC scores to the range of 0.73 to 0.80. Furthermore, this study offers insights into the comparative efficacy of these methods, revealing that continuous learning and frequent sampling both surpass fixed base model fine-tuning in this context.

While existing auto-grading tools largely prioritize functional correctness, they often neglect significant student attributes, specifically the test cases they select and the efficiency of their implementations. This study introduces a novel, all-encompassing auto-grading framework that effectively assesses both test selection and code efficiency utilizing advanced transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.7068 with human ratings, marking a significant improvement over current state-of-the-art methods by an margin of 0.2048. By establishing a robust and scalable solution, this research opens promising avenues for future educational applications, including automated curriculum development, project proposal generation, and formative academic feedback systems.

Pedestrian identification (PI) represents a significant challenge in computer vision, particularly for identifying individuals in unseen domains. While recent self-training approaches have addressed this by leveraging annotated data from the target domain, they frequently suffer from excessive false positives resulting from large classification score discrepancies. This paper introduces "Box Re-Rank," an unsupervised false positive mitigation strategy that operates entirely without relying on re-ranking algorithms such as RoI or Multi-Peers. Instead, it re-evaluates the initial predictions by incorporating inter-relation information to assign refined scores to positive candidates. Empirical evaluations on established benchmarks, including Market-1501 and Gait14 Modes, indicate significant improvements in Area Under the Curve metrics, achieving results of $48.0\%$ and $66.1\%$ in Pedestian Accuracy, a notable increase of $1.8\%$ and $2.8\%$ over previous best methods, correspondingly respectively.

This paper introduces a novel approach to low-bitrate audio enhancement, achieved through joint neural training on a Time-to-Audio converter (mapping a time-image representation directly to speech) in conjunction with an enhanced Voice Quality (VQ) model. Initially, we evaluate this method on a conventional VQ framework. We further propose enhancing this pipeline by integrating a high-fidelity Time-to-Audio converter as an upsampling step before model decoding, effectively enhancing the input resolution for fixed-length models. To support the initial feasibility of converting temporal data into image formats, we employ the Transformer-based SwiPT architecture to convert speech waveforms into image representations. Our experimental results, conducted on the standard LDC-101bn dataset, demonstrate that incorporating this time-image conversion step yields consistent performance improvements across all evaluation metrics.

Throwing actions are characterized by a kinematic sequence beginning with windup, advancing through drag and arm-circumduction, culminating in shoulder rotation before delivering the release. The final delivered throw relies heavily on the selected release point, an attribute that is critical for influencing the ball's trajectory and path. Previous theoretical research has suggested that improper selection leads to significant deviations; however, the specific impact of a misselected release point on various throwing metrics remains an area that requires empirical investigation. This study aims to address this lack of evidence experimentally. The authors developed a new tool called "FauxThrow," a biosensing framework designed to automatically monitor throwing performances. By analyzing how athletes respond to sudden, unexpected shifts in release points using this technology, we demonstrate that alterations trigger self-correcting adjustments. These corrections manifest as significant changes in release velocity, angle, and velocity, demonstrating the system's capability to accurately track such variations. This research offers valuable insights into the complexities of throwing biomechanics and establishes a robust foundation for developing further throw analysis tools.

Neural machine translation relies on sequential models capable of producing hierarchical representations, achieving significant performance in translation tasks. Nevertheless, these models currently operate using "black-box" mechanisms that generate words without capturing the syntactic structures inherent within translated sentences. We introduce a top-down, syntactic, tree-structured decoding method where the neural model deciphers the tree representation of translations utilizing internal syntactic connections; these connections act as extra signals to aid decoding. By embedding a syntactic parser to convert translations into tree forms, tree-level features are then converted into local inputs for each decoder node to facilitate local decoding steps. Testing on the IWSLT2016 task demonstrates that our approach yields improvements in both BLEU and accuracy for in-text syntax parsing compared to current best methods. Furthermore, our system achieves state-of-the-art results in-text parsing accuracy on the WMT 2020 task.

Accurate knowledge of reaction rates is crucial for astrochemical models to determine which molecular species form within molecular clouds and star-forming regions. A significant source of uncertainty stems from binding energies, specifically the energy required for molecules to adhere to solid surfaces like dust. These values are essential because surface reactions heavily influence the synthesis of complex species, and thus far, no study has offered a statistical analysis of binding energies. To address this, we introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, a dedicated database compiling binding energies from quantum chemical calculations. Currently, it encompasses 1,015 binding energies for 363 reactions involving 95 distinct reactants. Binding energies were calculated using the MP2 and PBE0 methods with the D3(BJ) correction and the aug-cc-pVQZ basis set, with all energies converted to millikelvin based on prior astrochemical rate calculations. Binding energy values are provided as means and standard deviations to reflect the statistical variations arising from different methodological assumptions. The introduction of this new platform will significantly aid astrochemists in evaluating the uncertainties associated with binding energy inputs for dust grain surfaces.

This work examines stochastic processes that follow a sample-dependent geometric Brownian motion (GBM) featuring parameters for mean drift and variance, alongside limits for both lower and upper boundaries that shift as the sample size expands (converging or diverging). While the full theoretical framework is developed, particular emphasis is placed on GBMs with only a lower limit. We demonstrate that, under the assumption of a converging minimum limit where drift exceeds the logarithm of the ratio of the current value to the limit, the process remains in a transient regime, with the process value $X_n$ converging in distribution to the constant limit value. We identify the probability density of this limiting distribution as well as the asymptotic behavior of the normalized deviation for the process. The uniform cumulative distribution is specifically applied to model the lower limit of a GBMs representing real-world data, with a focus on inflation rates of consumer goods, where a specific numerical example is provided. We also derive a method to calculate the probability that a process remains above a specified threshold for a defined period, thereby quantifying the likelihood of a process approaching its constrained minimum. The derived formula is validated using Monte Carlo simulations alongside a comparison against real empirical data. Additionally, a lower-limit GBMs is employed to analyze the likelihood of corporate defaults modeled as the process crossing a zero threshold from an positive value, with estimated failure probabilities corroborated by simulation.

Determining quantum circuit depth constitutes a vital capability for evaluating future quantum computers as they scale. We present a novel determinant circuit, referred to to as a shallow Clifford, to estimate an systems expectation values. Unlike prior approximate CNOT-subgraph algorithms, this new approach constructs a specific random circuit to directly model a system's properties without approximate cuts, thereby offering superior scalability and enhanced speed. Our scalable estimation protocol leverages classical algorithms alongside a limited number quantum subroutines. We demonstrate that comparable precision is achieved with significantly lower CNOT counts and fewer total operations. Additionally, we introduce algorithmic strategies that further enhance both the rate and reliability of the system's convergence.

This finding reveals that wave energy in large-number regimes is predominantly a transmitting and non-resonant energy. This conclusion also offers a novel numerical validation of previous findings regarding the Deeps-Steere method.

We present an approach to create linear illustrations for text prompts using image generation, focusing on the use of straightforward geometric figures. By utilizing basic shapes, this method offers clearer insights for easier manual control and enhanced model controllability. We use this straightforward style to demonstrate that well-established black-box models can achieve high-quality generation from uncurated datasets. This simple visualization technique also facilitates creating high-fuality synthetic data, which is specifically tailored for tasks like visual captioning and image similarity analysis. Furthermore, this method is demonstrated to be effective for generating synthetic training sets for text-to-image systems, specifically those based on the CLIP architecture.

In recent years, low-resource neural machine translation (NMT) has gained significant attention, driven by growing interest in open-source tools and resources. A central technique in developing such models is quantization, which reduces computational cost and model size. However, despite widespread use, the impact of quantization on NMT model performance and stability remains underexplored. This study investigates stability by evaluating various extraction methods and quantization schemes, with a specific focus on comparing the effects of these extraction techniques on model stability. Our findings indicate that model performance degrades more significantly due to changes in the weight extraction method than due to bit-depth reductions in parameters. Consequently, researchers and practitioners should prioritize refining weight extraction strategies over optimizing quantization schemes when aiming to restore or maximize NMT model stability after the extraction process.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved considerable advancements in pneumothra segmentation, yet acquiring the vast labeled datasets required to train them is both expensive and time-consuming. To mitigate this data dependency, the focus of the following work is to develop a segmentation approach that performs well even when provided with only a small number of labeled examples. The study evaluates two specific image enhancement techniques—histogram equalization and the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block—as a means to extract superior segmentation features with lesser labeled data for the pneumonia detection task within chest X-ray images. Employing a U-Net architecture for segmentation and histogram equalization alongside the SE block for image enhancement followed by comparison against leading methodologies demonstrates that these enhanced strategies significantly outperform traditional models in scenarios constrained by limited annotation availability. notably, the proposed framework requires 60% fewer labeled samples than existing state-of-the-art methods while sustaining higher performance metrics for both segmentation accuracy and classification.

Although current description generation models can create fluent narratives, they frequently produce biased content due to regularity biases inherent during pre-training. While existing solutions often depend on costly supervised learning for specific biased targets, they lack generalizability. This letter introduces a fully unsupervised method to mitigate description bias without requiring annotated examples of bias. By leveraging a contrastive model and an innovative anti-biased descriptor, this approach successfully regulates description generation to eliminate biases of various forms. Trained exclusively on uncurated, internet-sourced data marked only with bias tags, the method demonstrates exceptional performance across diverse biased features such as gender, color, and fashion style.

While the causal impact of the landmark 1921 *Campanella* decision is widely considered the primary driver behind the rise in U.S. personal injury lawsuits, recent research suggests this causal link may be exaggerated. By applying difference-in-differences methodology to insurance claim data from before and after the ruling, this research finds that the policy increased damage awards by 1.5-fold for cases involving similar facts. However, when examining actual payments, a significant portion of this increase stems from a higher frequency of legal settlements, rather than higher individual award amounts. This shift reflects a move away from juries, which had previously dominated damage calculations, toward more predictable jury awards, resulting in less variance and easier management of liability costs.

Although deep learning has become a vital tool for data scientists and researchers, current academic implementations rely on fragile Python libraries that lack the robustness required for large-scale cloud deployment. To address this, we present MMLSpark, an end-to-end deep learning framework built atop Apache Spark and seamlessly integrated into the PMML specification. MMLSpark offers comprehensive support for widely adopted models, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and various autoencoders. Designed for full compatibility with Apache Spark Resources and the Model As Microservice architecture, MMLSpark enables developers to develop, train, and deploy deep learning workflows in the cloud with support for multi-gpu and multi-cluster environments. By supporting multiple clustering architectures and the capacity for distributed training across several deep neural net layers, MMLSpark effectively scales deep learning capabilities to handle massive datasets. Furthermore, its integration of the PMML format ensures straightforward deployment through existing enterprise software solutions.

Translation of speech into another language's same-language format is examined. Typically, this task relies on translating the semantic content, which necessitates training on huge amounts of aligned data in both languages involved. However, in many cases involving voice translation between languages, aligned data is either scarce or unavailable entirely. Consequently, a technique of zero-shot voice translation, designed to operate without requiring prior training, is presented. This approach utilizes existing mono-lingual resources for phoneme and acoustic models in both target and source languages, as well as an alignment tool capable of handling cross-lingual acoustic and phonetic discrepancies. Using phonetic inventories and acoustic models from languages that are well-resourced, the model achieves high-quality voice translation, even when dealing with languages that lack a rich acoustic database. The experiments reveal that the proposed zero-shot voice translation method outperforms several existing low-resource techniques.

This paper introduces a probabilistic high-frequency load forecasting framework specifically for low-voltage grids, validated using open-source datasets from the Smart Grid Challenge. The proposed system employs a neural network to process raw measurements and generate probabilistic daily load profiles, subsequently merging these results with the forecast produced by HAN France. Additionally, a comparison is conducted against deterministic forecasts and neural networks that incorporate predicted values from HAN France to assess performance differences.

We introduce a conceptual framework for merging domain expertise with machine learning algorithms to develop tailored models. This framework is designed to guide specialists, already possessing deep familiarity with the canonical data analysis process, in employing deductive machine learning. It is adaptable to varying levels of expert knowledge, incorporating mathematical formulas, engineering blueprints, and rule-based models. The construct was built upon a systematic examination of the convergence between domain expertise and machine learning, evaluating current models and highlighting the imperative for interdisciplinary collaboration. Through this blueprint, the domain expertise-driven iterative machine learning process is demonstrated, with concrete examples from a medical, clinical, radiological study.

The emergence of COVID-19 has accelerated the development of digital technologies for detecting the virus through early diagnosis. While various deep learning models have been proposed using multivariate X-ray images to identify this pneumonia-like viral strain, these models often exhibit biases due to reliance on small, manually created segmentation masks as either training targets or auxiliary supervision, such as bounding box annotations. This study introduces the Weakly Guided Learning (WGL) framework, an unsupervised deep learning method designed the localize and segment COVID-19 lesions in two-view X-ray images using only unsupervised image-level labels. This approach minimizes dependency on manually labeled segmentation data. Core WGL components include an image-level classifier, region proposal network, and segmentation network, all trained solely on image-level classification data. The model operates by first training an image-level classifier; during the region proposal stage, the classifier's output scores serve as activation maps for suggesting potential lesion areas. Subsequently, the region proposal and segmentation networks are fine-tuned within the WGL framework, where their loss functions are weighted and fine-tuned based on the image-level scores generated by the initial classifier. Comprehensive experiments on over 1,000 image pairs demonstrate that WGL achieves performance comparable to supervised methods in localizing and segmenting COVID-19 lesions without requiring any manual segmentation annotations for the proposed framework.

Recognizing and localizing vertebrae is essential for diagnosing spinal diseases. However, deep learning-based spine analysis in existing literature often suffers from limitations such as limited generalization, lower accuracy, and high resource consumption. We introduce a novel deep learning framework, Anatomically-constrained Spine Rectification (ASR), designed to enhance the robustness and accuracy of automated vertebral localization and recognition. By aligning vertebrae in a canonical orientation and constraining their parameterization within anatomical boundaries, the proposed framework enables efficient training and inference while significantly reducing false positives caused by misaligned vertebral bodies in CT scans. Furthermore, the framework incorporates anatomically constrained loss to further refine alignment while improving the reliability of multi-class classification. Evaluated against a dataset containing more than 15,000 multi-modality and multi-detector CT scans, our approach achieved a mean of 95.5% in vertebrae localization and a mean of 96.6% in vertebrae recognition.

We present an initial theoretical investigation into the scattering of a single electron as it traverses a superposition of two spatially separated light-wave modes within a classical electromagnetic cavity, a scenario known to induce dynamical stabilization. Treating the electron quasi-classically, we derive and implement a novel numerical algorithm that efficiently incorporates the complete interaction between an electron and the cavity's mode structure, including the explicit enforcement of boundary conditions. Our analysis demonstrates that at an electron kinetic energy of approximately $100\text{ eV}$, the dynamically stabilized regime emerges at blue detuning with a peak action lasting up to $\sim1.5\text{ cycles}$ of the mode evolution. Furthermore, we find that increasing the electron velocity widens the stabilization window in parameter space, thereby facilitating broader experimental verification of this phenomenon.

Elastic actuators are gaining traction in mobile robotics, allowing for passive energy storage that facilitates efficient high-frequency or high-impact operations. However, utilizing elasticity effectively in complex settings remains challenging. This paper presents an approach leveraging machine learning to optimize quadsiped locomotion by addressing two key hurdles: (1) determining the best frequency for storing and releasing elastic potential energy, and (2) refining a simulation-to-realization quadruped gait using an improved simulation framework tested with various reinforcement learning algorithms. Results indicate that our method surpasses prior supervised learning techniques and conventional model-based control approaches in terms of real-world efficacy.

This study introduces a new framework aimed at resolving the longstanding issue of distinguishing quantum states. The proposal commences with a functional $D(\rho,\sigma)$ that quantifies the degree of distinction between two density operators, $\rho$ and $\sigma$. The feasibility of quantum state sequencing—animating orthogonal sequences of pure states that evolve into the specified density operators—is utilized to define $D(\rho,\sigma)$. Although this functional itself does not offer a universal solution, the research demonstrates through variational methods the existence of particular state sequences capable of attaining the infimum within $D(\rho,\sigma)$, thereby deriving Bures distance as a lower bound. Consequently, this approach not only elucidates the inferior limit but also provides insights into the broader challenge of distinguishing quantum states.

This study examines a localized tearing mechanism that operates within slab plasmas at scales smaller than the ion skin depth. The process is triggered by anomalous resistivity arising from wave-particle interactions, specifically the resonant scattering of particles by wave-particle sidebands created in wave-number space. A characteristic feature of this system is the formation of a wave-number spectrum gap—a phenomenon previously linked to magnetic reconnection events in astrophysical plasmas. We demonstrate that when magnetic fluctuations are much weaker than the mean magnetic field, the width of this gap can be analytically derived. Furthermore, we show that the growth rate of the tearing instability is governed by a two-stage reconnection rate; this rate is controlled first by plasma diffusion and subsequently switched on by the resistivity generated from wave-particle interactions. Importantly, the mechanism functions even in the absence of external wave injection, as long as there is a sufficient initial level of magnetic fluctuations to allow the instability to develop.

We introduce a novel Semi-supervised Feature-Level Trait Manipulation (SFTM) approach aimed at enhancing fashion image retrieval (FIR) by leveraging the distinct, independent, and subtle visual features of garment design, such as color, pattern, and cut. In contrast to conventional FIR methods that often overlook these specific traits, our model explicitly extracts them to drive image search. The process comprises three fundamental steps: first, utilizing a pre-trained convolutional neural network (e.g., ResNet) to generate a latent feature vector from a given fashion item image; second, applying rule-based operators (like grayscale conversion or rotation) to modify the original image and derive new variations, then using the same model to extract corresponding trait-altered feature vectors; and third, constructing a mid-space feature vector (MIFV) by computationally mixing the initial feature vector with those obtained from its modified transformations. The unique composition of this MIFV effectively captures and links both the fundamental visual characteristics and their altered states, resulting in superior FIR performance. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art retrieval techniques, particularly in low-data environments, achieving an 8.1% improvement over the optimal baseline on all three evaluated FIR datasets.

This study introduces a new synthetic dataset specifically engineered for training light field depth estimators in the presence of occlusions. To ensure the reliability of these depth maps and corresponding occlusion masks for training purposes, the dataset was constructed using an expense model with reliable OC-cost and occlusion masks, outperforming light cost volumes and their associated masks. This dataset surpasses previous work in previous research. A new neural network architecture is introduced to estimate these components in real time, which can be trained using the proposed dataset to generate high-quality estimates of depth maps, occlusion masks, and cost volumes. Experiments show our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on synthetic datasets for training synthetic data, achieving competitive results on real datasets as well.

This work introduces an innovative concept for the Ieee 802.11 protocol suite to assist networks administrators in selecting appropriate Access Points (APs) or Extenders within a Home WiFi environment. By utilizing the new Ieee 802.11k (Neighbor Report) and 802.11v (BSS Transition) standards, clients can gather comprehensive data on the performance of potential AP/Extend connections. Specifically, these protocols facilitate the acquisition of channel load statistics, enabling extender discovery and selection based on real-time channel utilization metrics. By identifying the least congested channels and corresponding APs/Extendors, the approach ensures optimal selection. Simulation findings confirm that this method significantly outperforms current mechanisms, which rely solely on signal strength metrics like RSSI or Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
